Table Mountain Safety Risks

By: Michael Duffett | Production

Proposal


Show:

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
The dedicated band of rescuers at full speed on Table Mountain.

Unique Selling Point:
Table Mountain, of the iconic tourist sites of the word, is a huge wildness and a favourite amongst hiker. Access to it is unlimited – and since lockdown there has been an explosion of people walking up the mountain. Lions head at times had become unmanageable as a result of evening climb that people take to drink their sundowners perched on the rocks.

Many new people who decide to walk up the mountain, sometimes at the spur of the moment, are ill equipped – they wear the wrong clothes, they may be in flip flops, they don't take enough water.

It is inevitable that more people on the mountain, the more incidents – and we must ask ourselves if any of these can have been prevented. A main focus of this story are the rescue operations.


Summary:
According to Johann Marais, spokes person of the Wilderness Search and Rescue, over weekends, they are responding to as many as 5 distress calls per day. One one day a few weeks ago the emergency helicopter was called out twice. The unspoken heroes are these dedicated rescuers who rush everything to save lives, help distressed people off the mountain or face death on narrow ledges as they retrieve bodies.

We peek into the lives of these rescuers – from the moment they get a distress call, to the end of their mission which may include trauma counselling. We see what happens once the call is made. The medics and an advance team are dispatched and they sprint up the mountain. The person directing is from a control room in town. In the mean time a doctor from Emergency is making his way to the scene with another group of rescuers, many of whom got the call whilst at work. Another group, the private radio club are also despatched to set up comms. We speak to a helicopter pilot as well and hopefully fly with him. We also see how the new drone works, that looks for victims.


Further information:
We speak to two families who lost loved ones. In December while on holiday in the cape, a JHB gamily nearly reached the peak when Mrs Talia fell, and could not be resuscitated by rescuers. She was flown off the mountain. She died in front of her husband and two small children. They wrote a heart felt thanks to the rescue teams.

Last week two more tragedies, which also proves that even the most experienced runners and hikers can become victims. A lovely man Kim lives for the mountain – the type of person who would sprint up and down the mountain before breakfast and then go to work. He fell 100 meters to his death.

We show the increase of incidents as the mountain swells with the new hikers and ask SANParks if more can be done to prevent incidents. Where are their full page ads in the news papers warning visitors and new hikers to take precautions? What about the maintenance of paths , some of which have fallen into dis-repair?

Script:


TABLE MOUNTAIN

VO (00:00):
It's the playground of serious mountaineers, rock climbers, abseilers, trail runners. The iconic table mountain is also a favorite destination for 100/s of 1000’s of hikers that climb it every year. Zaheer and Zarena Talia from Johannesburg had been looking foreard to climbing the mountain again with their children.

Zaheer (00:20):
So it had always been my dream to take my kids up again. So we'd been discussing this for the last year.
VO (00:26):

The 19th of December, 2020 was a beautiful day. The route the Talias chose was skeleton Gorge, popular amongst hikers

Zaheer (00:36):
It was just some stunning views. And we walk in in a fashion where I lead my kids walk in the middle and my wife brings up from the back.

The mountain was teaming with fellow hikers that day.

The easing of COVID restrictions has seen a huge increase in hikers and experienced Mountaineer Fiona Mcintosh noticed the surge, especially when beaches were closed in December, 2020,

Fiona (01:02):
There was a hell of a lot of traffic on the mountain, and a lot of people who are less experienced and I think particularly on lion's head and our platteklip Gorge, the main routes. There was a lot of overcrowding.

The Talia family had almost reached the top of the mountain When Zarena collapsed.
Zaheer (07:27):

She was lagging behind. I heard a scream and she had had a heart attack or something related to her heart which had resulted in just falling down.

VO (07:39):
A doctor and t wo paramedics who were hiking close by tried to resuscitate Zarena.

Zaheer (07:44):
And by the time mountain rescue arrived, they had informed me that she had passed away and it was difficult and it was really, really difficult.

VO (01:16):

REPLACE: Just this year, the table mountain chain, which consists of lion's head, often jam packed with hikers, table mountain and the South Peninsula Ranges has seen over 50 rescue operations. Alister Christians commander of the Metro rescue base near Pinelands has had his hands full

WITH THIS: This year alone the Table Mountain chain has seen more than 50 rescue operations… from Lion’s Head, which is often jam-packed with hikers, across the mountain to the South Peninsula ranges. Alister Christians is rescue manager of the Cape Town metropole.

Alistaire (01:35):
In the last two weeks. We had four to five calls per day on the table mountain or on Lion's Head. That is only here in the metropole.

VO (01:46):
In Feb, Experienced hiker Ulrike Kuschke was descending the mountain with friends on the nursery ravine route when she fell.

Ulrike (01:52):
Lost my footing and fell in the path but in such a way that I tumbled and rolled and then came to a standstill.

VO (02:04):
She immediately knew she was in trouble. Her hip was broken. A call went out for help and soon SanParks Rangers, and other rescuers appeared on the scene. She was carried uphill to an area for safe evacuation and then air lifted off the mountain and taken to hospital, where she underwent a hip replacement operation.

Ulrike (02:26):
It's amazing where, where do these guys come from? And they do it with such compassion and care

VO (02:36):
It starts with a distress call coming into the EMS provincial emergency control center.

Dr De Vries (02:40):
Particularly when it's on the mountain. There's a sense of urgency. The health operations center ensures that we mobilize multiple people because an operation of this nature requires many stakeholders.

VO (02:53):
On 20th of March at 08h00??? the control centre patched through an emergency call to the Metro rescue base.

83 year old Traves Nettleton had been hiking in a large group to the Cecilia forest waterfall when he missed his footing…fell and rolled down the mountain for about 15 meters.

The incident commander sent out a WhatsApp message to Wilderness Search and Rescue, which comprises multi-disciplinary volunteer organisations… and role-players like Sanparks, the police and South African RED CROSS AIR MERCY SERVICE.

A Metro Rescue vehicle was dispatched and set up base at Constantia Neck. The OFF-ROAD RESCUE UNIT ferries Metro paramedics and other rescuers to a site close to Nettleton’s position…where he was stabilized and his wounds treated.

This operation was coordinated entirely on the WhatsApp group and in all, seven organizations participated.

Nettleton (04:03):
You're in safe hands. I'm in very good hands yes. Absolutely amazed. Yes, I really, really am. How good care I've been taken of.

VO (04:14):
Team leaders decided to airlift Nettleton off the mountain. Western Cape Heath contracted the South African Red Cross Air Mercy Service, which has been involved in over a 800 search and rescue missions on this Mountain chain. Their helicopters can be airborne within five minutes of a call.

Pilot (04:33):
You always put yourself in the patient's shoes and you want to get there as soon as possible to provide the best source of help you can give them.

VO (04:41):
The helicopter arrived just after 1 pm and lowered a stretcher to one of the rescuers below… it landed close-by while the team spent the next 20 minutes preparing their patient for an aerial evacuation.

Medic (04:57):083 793 2457
I want you to just keep your eyes closed as much as possible for me, there's a lot of dust flying around and just keep your eyes closed.

VO (05:04):
Then helicopter returned and hoisted up one of the paramedics to take care of Nettelton on board. The cable was again lowered and he was then successfully airlifted off the mountain and taken to hospital. Volunteer rescuers have day jobs, but they ARE prepared to drop everything to assist in a rescue…often dangerous and tiring work. Pastor Brent Russel is always on standby.

Brent (05:35):
So I've been rock climbing for about 20 years, and I think that affords us a measure of technical ability in the mountains. And I just think I've got a huge skill set at my disposal that can help save people's lives. And there's just nothing better than being able to do that.

VO (05:49):
Fiona who is an adventure travel writer, has climbed many mountains around the world.

Masa (05:54):
Tell me why do you do this?

Fiona (05:56):
Well, it's really a chance to give something back. And I guess to be honest, if I got into trouble, I'd hope people came looking for me. So I'm very happy to go looking for them.

VO (06:06):
And they have their hands full : statistics show that falls, hikers becoming stuck and tired are the main reasons for rescues this year. Too often, hikers are taking to the mountain without the correct gear. They stray off path. They don't take enough water and become dehydrated, or they suffer hypothermia because clothing worn is inadequate for the changing weather conditions. Assisting rescuers now is the Metro rescue base's new drone, which came into operation in December, 2020. On the 10th of February, a hiker became stranded on a rock ledge on lion's head. A distress call was received at 10:35 AM.

Drone Pilot (06:48):
We making the search and rescue time, a lot easier and a lot quicker for patients to be removed off the mountain successfully.

VO (06:55):
The drone took off at 12:43 PM. Within 5 minutes, it had found the hiker and rescuers were then guided to him and he was led to safety, but sometimes rescuers have to brace themselves for the worst case scenario.

LINK (07:10):
Tragically every year hikers and even experienced mountaineers lose their lives on the Table Mountain chain.

VO:
Last year there were 9 fatalities, Zarina Talier being one of them. A rescue operation swung into action and she was airlifted off the mountain and the devastated family was driven down the mountain on a jeep track. A trauma counsellor had been called in to stand by. (the acronyms don’t help – you’ve already said which organisations are in the group)

Zaheer (08:00):
A counselor there already waiting for my kids, which I found was really wonderful. Just to be able to firstly, just assess a little bit on myself and then also just to be able to give me a little bit of feedback in terms of the kids. It's it's, it's, it's all overwhelming at that point.

VO (08:17):
This year has seen six fatalities on the Table Mountain chain so far. Russel is often tasked with retrieving bodies from inaccessible locations.

Brent (08:28):
Look that's always difficult. And I think each rescuer their has their own mechanism to deal with that. We do check up on each other because these things are traumatic, but then you're helping a family find closure. You know, otherwise they they've lost a loved one and they can't find that that solace and that closure at the end. And so whilst that's a very difficult and painful part of our rescue, we do it because we know it helps those families.

VO (08:48):
In January, a letter written by the Talia family was published in the press, thanking all of those who had assisted them during their difficult time. Kuschke is recovering well… she never realised that volunteers played such a key part in the process.

Ulrike (09:04):
These were all really complete strangers and they all showed me the best side of humanity, but why are they so quiet? We never hear about them

VO (09:16):
WILDERNESS SEARCH & RESCUE’s Johan Marais says volunteers prefer it that way.

Johan (09:22):
We believe that the, the, the, the best recognition that we get is the fact that we are successful in what we do.

VO (09:31):
In the meantime, Traves Nettleton has been discharged from hospital – he’s doing well and grateful to those who helped him.

Dr De Vries (09:39):
It's quite humbling to think that... I mean, this is my job, you know, I mean, I, I get paid to do this as do most of my team. It's when we are encountered such commitment from people who don't get paid and it's not easy work, you know it's dangerous work. So it's, it's quite remarkable. The level of, of, I guess, humanity that these volunteers demonstrate.

Pilot (04:33): You always put yourself in the patient's shoes and you want to get there as soon as possible to provide the best source of help you can give them. VO (04:41): The helicopter arrived just after 1 pm and lowered a stretcher to one of the rescuers below… it landed close-by while the team spent the next 20 minutes preparing their patient for an aerial evacuation. Medic (04:57):083 793 2457 I want you to just keep your eyes closed as much as possible for me, there's a lot of dust flying around and just keep your eyes closed. VO (05:04): Then helicopter returned and hoisted up one of the paramedics to take care of Nettelton on board. The cable was again lowered and he was then successfully airlifted off the mountain and taken to hospital. Volunteer rescuers have day jobs, but they ARE prepared to drop everything to assist in a rescue…often dangerous and tiring work. Pastor Brent Russel is always on standby. Brent (05:35): So I've been rock climbing for about 20 years, and I think that affords us a measure of technical ability in the mountains. And I just think I've got a huge skill set at my disposal that can help save people's lives. And there's just nothing better than being able to do that. VO (05:49): Fiona who is an adventure travel writer, has climbed many mountains around the world. Masa (05:54): Tell me why do you do this? Fiona (05:56): Well, it's really a chance to give something back. And I guess to be honest, if I got into trouble, I'd hope people came looking for me. So I'm very happy to go looking for them. VO (06:06): And they have their hands full : statistics show that falls, hikers becoming stuck and tired are the main reasons for rescues this year. Too often, hikers are taking to the mountain without the correct gear. They stray off path. They don't take enough water and become dehydrated, or they suffer hypothermia because clothing worn is inadequate for the changing weather conditions. Assisting rescuers now is the Metro rescue base's new drone, which came into operation in December, 2020. On the 10th of February, a hiker became stranded on a rock ledge on lion's head. A distress call was received at 10:35 AM. Drone Pilot (06:48): We making the search and rescue time, a lot easier and a lot quicker for patients to be removed off the mountain successfully. VO (06:55): The drone took off at 12:43 PM. Within 5 minutes, it had found the hiker and rescuers were then guided to him and he was led to safety, but sometimes rescuers have to brace themselves for the worst case scenario. LINK (07:10): Tragically every year hikers and even experienced mountaineers lose their lives on the Table Mountain chain. VO: Last year there were 9 fatalities, Zarina Talier being one of them. A rescue operation swung into action and she was airlifted off the mountain and the devastated family was driven down the mountain on a jeep track. A trauma counsellor had been called in to stand by. (the acronyms don’t help – you’ve already said which organisations are in the group) Zaheer (08:00): A counselor there already waiting for my kids, which I found was really wonderful. Just to be able to firstly, just assess a little bit on myself and then also just to be able to give me a little bit of feedback in terms of the kids. It's it's, it's, it's all overwhelming at that point. VO (08:17): This year has seen six fatalities on the Table Mountain chain so far. Russel is often tasked with retrieving bodies from inaccessible locations. Brent (08:28): Look that's always difficult. And I think each rescuer their has their own mechanism to deal with that. We do check up on each other because these things are traumatic, but then you're helping a family find closure. You know, otherwise they they've lost a loved one and they can't find that that solace and that closure at the end. And so whilst that's a very difficult and painful part of our rescue, we do it because we know it helps those families. VO (08:48): In January, a letter written by the Talia family was published in the press, thanking all of those who had assisted them during their difficult time. Kuschke is recovering well… she never realised that volunteers played such a key part in the process. Ulrike (09:04): These were all really complete strangers and they all showed me the best side of humanity, but why are they so quiet? We never hear about them VO (09:16): WILDERNESS SEARCH & RESCUE’s Johan Marais says volunteers prefer it that way. Johan (09:22): We believe that the, the, the, the best recognition that we get is the fact that we are successful in what we do. VO (09:31): In the meantime, Traves Nettleton has been discharged from hospital – he’s doing well and grateful to those who helped him. Dr De Vries (09:39): It's quite humbling to think that... I mean, this is my job, you know, I mean, I, I get paid to do this as do most of my team. It's when we are encountered such commitment from people who don't get paid and it's not easy work, you know it's dangerous work. So it's, it's quite remarkable. The level of, of, I guess, humanity that these volunteers demonstrate.

metadata.One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...): The dedicated band of rescuers at full speed on Table Mountain.
metadata.Unique Selling Point: Table Mountain, of the iconic tourist sites of the word, is a huge wildness and a favourite amongst hiker. Access to it is unlimited – and since lockdown there has been an explosion of people walking up the mountain. Lions head at times had become unmanageable as a result of evening climb that people take to drink their sundowners perched on the rocks. Many new people who decide to walk up the mountain, sometimes at the spur of the moment, are ill equipped – they wear the wrong clothes, they may be in flip flops, they don't take enough water. It is inevitable that more people on the mountain, the more incidents – and we must ask ourselves if any of these can have been prevented. A main focus of this story are the rescue operations.
metadata.Summary: According to Johann Marais, spokes person of the Wilderness Search and Rescue, over weekends, they are responding to as many as 5 distress calls per day. One one day a few weeks ago the emergency helicopter was called out twice. The unspoken heroes are these dedicated rescuers who rush everything to save lives, help distressed people off the mountain or face death on narrow ledges as they retrieve bodies. We peek into the lives of these rescuers – from the moment they get a distress call, to the end of their mission which may include trauma counselling. We see what happens once the call is made. The medics and an advance team are dispatched and they sprint up the mountain. The person directing is from a control room in town. In the mean time a doctor from Emergency is making his way to the scene with another group of rescuers, many of whom got the call whilst at work. Another group, the private radio club are also despatched to set up comms. We speak to a helicopter pilot as well and hopefully fly with him. We also see how the new drone works, that looks for victims.
metadata.Further information: We speak to two families who lost loved ones. In December while on holiday in the cape, a JHB gamily nearly reached the peak when Mrs Talia fell, and could not be resuscitated by rescuers. She was flown off the mountain. She died in front of her husband and two small children. They wrote a heart felt thanks to the rescue teams. Last week two more tragedies, which also proves that even the most experienced runners and hikers can become victims. A lovely man Kim lives for the mountain – the type of person who would sprint up and down the mountain before breakfast and then go to work. He fell 100 meters to his death. We show the increase of incidents as the mountain swells with the new hikers and ask SANParks if more can be done to prevent incidents. Where are their full page ads in the news papers warning visitors and new hikers to take precautions? What about the maintenance of paths , some of which have fallen into dis-repair?
